analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 0.1% tax on trades of stocks, bonds, and derivatives.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 6 senators' support and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 0.1% excise tax on every purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded in the U.S. or involving U.S. parties. A $10,000 stock purchase would carry a $10 tax, paid through the exchange or broker. It exempts new stock issues and very short-term debt, and it taxes deals routed through foreign subsidiaries owned by U.S. shareholders so the tax can't be dodged by trading offshore. The revenue would go to the Treasury; the bill does not earmark it for any specific purpose.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the federal Treasury would gain a new revenue stream drawn from high-volume securities trading. Because the tax is charged per transaction, its burden falls heaviest on firms and investors that trade constantly — high-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, and large institutional traders — while a long-term investor who buys a few times a year pays very little.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises revenue from securities trading rather than from wages or ordinary consumption, since the tax is charged on each purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative [S2][S3].
Because the tax is per-transaction, an investor who trades rarely pays far less than a firm executing thousands of trades per second, concentrating the burden on high-volume traders [S2][S3].

The bill includes anti-avoidance rules: purchases by a U.S. person or on a U.S. exchange are covered even if other parties are foreign, controlled foreign corporations are treated as U.S. persons with the tax paid by their U.S. shareholders, and the Treasury Secretary must write regulations to prevent routing trades through non-U.S. parties [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-volume financial traders — hedge funds, high-frequency trading firms, and large institutions — would pay the tax directly on each purchase. Exchanges and brokers would be responsible for collecting it. Some of the cost could trickle to ordinary investors as slightly wider trading costs, and reduced trading could mean marginally lower liquidity and returns in retirement accounts.

drawbacks.text: A per-trade tax is passed into trading costs, so some portion would land on ordinary investors' 401(k)s and index funds, which buy and sell constantly as money flows in and out [S2][S3].
Taxes on each transaction discourage some trading, which critics argue reduces market liquidity and could make it slightly more expensive for savers to buy and sell [S2].
The bill does not earmark its revenue, so there is no guarantee the money would fund anything specific for ordinary people [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: the tax raises money in a way that falls mostly on the most active and wealthiest market participants, but a share of the cost leaks into the retirement accounts of ordinary savers through slightly higher trading costs. The design reduces that leakage — short-term debt is exempt, and trades by insurers and ordinary commodity hedgers are carved out — but it does not eliminate it, and the revenue has no designated purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on July 25, 2023, with five Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Van Hollen, Warren, Merkley, Whitehouse, and Fetterman [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firms that profit from massive trading volume — high-frequency trading shops, hedge funds, and large institutions — are better off, since they never faced the tax. The exchanges and brokers that would have collected it also avoided the compliance burden.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-volume trading firms and hedge funds

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 6 of 48 Senate Democrats — and no Republican support appears in the record; the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote.

industries.industry: High-frequency trading firms and hedge funds
industries.note: A 0.1% tax on every purchase would come directly out of the thin margins these firms earn on enormous trading volume, so their interest ran squarely against the bill. Their cost would otherwise be a new revenue source for the Treasury.

Exchanges and brokers would be legally responsible for collecting and remitting the tax on every covered purchase, adding compliance costs. Some of that cost, and any reduced trading volume, would flow to their customers and revenues.

industries.industry: Large institutional investors and asset managers
industries.note: Mutual funds and index funds trade constantly on behalf of savers, so a per-purchase tax would raise their costs slightly. The burden is small per trade but recurring.
